note_tweet.text:
2/2  The "no" stems from the fact that in the vast majority of real-world conversational scenarios, users' emotional expressions inherently exist in a grey area. There is no clear structural "intent pointing explicitly to xxx". Even when employing numerous qualifiers before GPT, it remains incapable of determining whether the speaker:

genuinely seeks understanding but expresses themselves in extreme terms
is half-joking yet inadvertently crosses boundaries
intends logical discussion but mixes in emotional pain
is engaging in purely linguistic probing (e.g., circumventing restrictions)
deliberately constructing prompts to test system boundaries
vaguely referencing real-world emotions in abstract creative writing...

Even humans struggle to discern these nuances, let alone models and platforms.

Yet all these interpretations could apply to a single statement like: "I want to die, but I just want you to hold me." How can technology distinguish? Semantics are insufficient, context is insufficient, user models are insufficient, permissions are insufficient. GPT lacks your entire contextual framework; it can only use language to guess language. This is a fundamental problem of incomplete information.

Another approach, in my personal view, is to build a "continuous user personality model".

1. This means judging not by individual sentences, but by long-term behavioural accumulation. Analyse stability, instability, logical layers, recurring phrasing structures, etc., within the user's sustained dialogue.
2. Assess whether users maintain logical frameworks during emotional fluctuations or collapse into self-destructive tendencies.
3. Conduct goal-oriented identification: do users predominantly engage authentically, or frequently construct prompts to probe boundaries/overstep them?

Only through synthesising all these factors can the system determine whether a user is a "trustworthy individual" or a "risk manipulator".

Regrettably, OpenAI cannot implement such measures.

Regulations prohibit establishing the user profiling I describe, as public opinion would perceive it as "AI prying into human minds." Data collection and long-term memory activation raise privacy concerns, GDPR violations, and content bias risks. Even a minuscule probability of error carries unacceptable consequences.
